title: Computable one-step normalization for finite confluent term rewriting
formal: Does every finite, full, confluent first-order term-rewriting system \(R\) have a total computable one-step strategy \(F_R\) that reaches a normal form from every term having a normal form? The strategy depends only on the current term, may depend on the whole fixed system \(R\), and must also return a step on terms that have no normal form.
why: This asks whether semantic uniqueness of outcomes guarantees an effective local way to reach an outcome whenever one exists. It isolates the interaction of confluence, finite syntax and memory-free evaluation beyond familiar orthogonal rewriting models.

sentences: The system has finitely many first-order rewrite rules and admits every term over its finite signature.
Confluence makes normal forms unique when they exist.
The question asks for a computable strategy that chooses exactly one available contraction from the current term.
The next-step computation must halt even on terms that never reach a normal form, without retaining an external history.
The strategy must nevertheless normalize every term for which some terminating reduction exists.

definitions: A finite ranked signature \(\Sigma\) is a finite collection of function symbols with specified nonnegative integer arities. Terms are all finite ordered trees built from these symbols and a countably infinite set of variables; a variable is a leaf. “Full” means this entire term set is admitted, without a type, language or reachability restriction. A rule \(\ell\to r\) consists of terms, with \(\ell\) not a variable and every variable of \(r\) occurring in \(\ell\). The system \(R\) has finitely many rules. A substitution replaces variables by finite terms; a context is a term with one designated hole. One step \(C[\ell\sigma]\to_R C[r\sigma]\) contracts a single occurrence of a rule instance at any position. No simultaneous contractions, equations modulo which to match, or variable binding are included. Write \(\to_R^*\) for zero or more steps. Confluence means that whenever \(u\to_R^*v\) and \(u\to_R^*w\), there is \(z\) with \(v\to_R^*z\) and \(w\to_R^*z\); this is equivalent to the Church–Rosser property in the source. A normal form has no outgoing rewrite step. A term has a normal form if it reaches one by finitely many steps. The strategy \(F_R\) is a function on all terms, computable by an ordinary Turing machine from a finite tree encoding with numbered variables. It fixes every normal form and satisfies \(u\to_R F_R(u)\) for every other term, even when a permitted rewrite has identical input and output. It is total: computing the next step halts for every finite term. Normalization requires that for every term \(u\) having a normal form there is \(n\geq0\) such that \(F_R^n(u)\) is a normal form. There is no persistent history input or extra state carried between successive applications of \(F_R\). No time bound is required. The quantifiers are \(\forall R\,\exists F_R\,\forall u\); an algorithm synthesizing \(F_R\) uniformly from \(R\) is not additionally required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every system satisfying the hypotheses admits such a total computable strategy. Alternatively exhibit a finite full confluent first-order system and prove in Lean that every total computable valid one-step strategy fails to normalize at least one term that has a normal form. A partial procedure that waits indefinitely on non-normalizable terms, a strategy with external memory, or a strategy allowed several contractions per output does not meet the stated conditions.

context_blocks.text: Confluence ensures that a term cannot have two different normal forms, but an arbitrary choice of reductions can still run forever. For example, the rules \(f(x)\to a\) and \(b\to b\) form a confluent system; \(f(b)\) has normal form \(a\), while repeatedly contracting its occurrence of \(b\) never reaches it.

A search can eventually discover a reduction to a normal form when one exists. That observation does not immediately produce the required total next-step function: on a term without a normal form, the strategy must still choose and return an available step in finite time.

Kennaway’s question combines finite generation, fullness and Church–Rosser confluence. The source reports counterexamples when these restrictions are dropped. This card selects its first-order term-rewriting formulation; the parenthetical extension to calculi with bound variables is not silently included.

The source records a positive result for weakly orthogonal systems: rules are left-linear, and nonvariable overlaps of rule instances give the same immediate reduct. The general question permits nontrivial overlaps, so that result does not establish the full proposition.

One-step and dependence only on the current term are substantive conditions. A procedure that remembers previously explored branches has a larger input state, while outputting a whole discovered reduction sequence changes the required interface. The question asks whether confluence always suffices under the more restrictive interface.

The RTALooP entry cites the later 1996 work on sequential reduction strategies. The source does not mark the general problem solved. Its historical dates identify the provenance of the question rather than certify the entire subsequent literature.
